# Two-dimensional wave equation {#sec-wave2d}

`apps/wave2d` — the reference for **coupled first-order systems** and for
mixed boundary conditions.

## Physical setting

Acoustic propagation on a two-dimensional slab. The application is the
smallest shipped example of two prognostic fields advanced together, and of a
domain that is periodic in one direction and physically bounded in the other.

The physical question is a waveguide question: **release a pulse in a slab
bounded by two walls — how does it reflect, and does the character of the
reflection depend on whether the wall is rigid or pressure-releasing?** A
Dirichlet wall inverts the reflected pulse; a Neumann wall does not.
@fig-wave2d-walls is that question answered from a pair of runs. The
observable the application nominally reports is the **interior RMS of the
displacement field**, `global_rms_u_interior`, together with the CFL number
$c\Delta t/\Delta x$ it ran at; see the note below on what that number
actually contains. Snapshots of $u$ can be written as VTK for visual
inspection of the reflection itself, which is what the figure uses.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `global_rms_u_interior` is always zero

The interior sum skips `half_width` cells on *every* axis, including $z$ —
and this application is an $n_z = 1$ slab, so the $z$ loop is empty and the
reduction runs over no cells at all. Both CPU drivers therefore print
`global_rms_u_interior=0` for every configuration, which is what a run of
either binary in this repository does today. The field itself is correct;
only this summary line is not. Until it is fixed, the VTK series is the only
thing this application reports about its solution.
:::

## Problem setup

Command-line driven, no JSON, and no science preset: every configuration of
this application is a demonstration or a test. It is worth being explicit that
the application **reports no error against any reference solution** — unlike
@sec-heat3d, its summary line was meant to carry an amplitude, not an
accuracy, and as noted above it currently carries neither.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Use case | A pulse reflecting between the two walls of an acoustic slab, as the smallest coupled two-field example in the report |
| Domain | $N_x \times N_y \times 1$ slab with $\Delta x = \Delta y = 1$, origin at $(0,0,0)$. Defaults $N_x = N_y = 64$ |
| Grid | `Nx Ny n_steps dt [fd_order] y_bc [u_wall]`; defaults 200 steps at $\Delta t = 0.01$, second order. `fd_order` must be even in $[2,20]$ for `wave2d_fd`; the manual and device drivers are fixed at second order. In practice only order 2 runs: the halo width must fit in *every* owned dimension and this is an $n_z = 1$ slab, so order 4 and above abort in `pfc::halo::create_padded_face_types_6` before the first step. VTK output cadence is `--vtk-every`, default every step |
| Boundary conditions | **Periodic in $x$** by MPI halo exchange; **physical in $y$**, either homogeneous Dirichlet ($u = u_{\mathrm{wall}}$ and $v = 0$ on the wall, imposed by an odd mirror of the ghost cells *and* by writing the owned boundary cells directly) or homogeneous Neumann (even mirror). The $y$ correction runs after the unconditional periodic exchange and overwrites the ghost values it produced |
| Initial condition | A centred Gaussian bump in $u$ with $v = 0$: $\sigma = 0.12\min(N_x,N_y)$, centred at $(\tfrac12(N_x-1), \tfrac12(N_y-1))$. Each test picks its own $\sigma$; there is no single canonical parameter set across the application |
| Key physical parameters | Wave speed $c = 1$ exactly, a compile-time constant not exposed on the command line. $u_{\mathrm{wall}}$ defaults to 0 and only affects Dirichlet runs. Nondimensional throughout |
| Observable | `global_rms_u_interior` (always 0 today — see the note in *Physical setting*); `cfl_c_dt_dx`; `timing_s` and `avg_step_time_s`; optional VTK series of $u$ |
| Model maturity | numerical verification: **manufactured** and **regression** — the temporal order of the RK2 and RK4 steppers is measured against a self-generated fine-timestep RK4 reference, not a closed form, and the remaining coverage is a pinned CPU checksum, CPU-vs-device parity, and boundary ghost values checked by hand · physical completeness: **canonical** — this is the constant-coefficient scalar wave equation, with no damping, no heterogeneous medium and no source term · calibration: **none** |

The two directions mean different things, which is the point of the
application. Periodicity in $x$ makes the slab infinitely long, or equivalently
a ring: a pulse that leaves the right edge arrives at the left, so there is no
along-slab attenuation and no far field. The $y$ walls are the physically
interesting idealisation. Dirichlet is a pressure-release boundary — the
reflected pulse comes back inverted — and Neumann is a rigid one, reflecting
without inversion. **Neither absorbs.** There is no radiation condition and no
absorbing layer anywhere in the application, so energy put into the slab never
leaves it, and a long run is a reverberant box rather than a propagation
experiment. Anything about how a wave escapes into open water or open air is
outside this model.

## Governing equations

The second-order wave equation $u_{tt} = c^2\nabla^2 u$ is written as a
coupled first-order system in displacement and velocity:

$$
\partial_t u \;=\; v,
\qquad
\partial_t v \;=\; c^2\,\nabla^2 u ,
$$ {#eq-w2-pde}

with $\nabla^2 = \partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}$ on an $n_z = 1$ slab.

Writing it this way is what lets a single stepper advance a tuple of
increments $(\mathrm{d}u, \mathrm{d}v)$, which is the pattern any multi-field
application reuses.

## Boundary conditions

Periodic in $x$, handled by MPI halo exchange. In $y$ the slab is
physically bounded, with **Dirichlet**
($u = u_{\mathrm{wall}}$, default 0, and $v = 0$ on the wall) or **Neumann**
($\partial_y u = 0$) conditions applied as a ghost-cell correction after the
periodic exchange. Both are second-order cell-centred mirrors — odd about
$u_{\mathrm{wall}}$ for Dirichlet, even for Neumann — and a mirrored index that
would fall outside the local extent is an error rather than a clamp.

The ordering matters: the exchange is unconditional and the physical
correction overwrites the ghost values it produced on the boundary faces. This
keeps the mixed case from needing a separate communication pattern.

## Finite-difference formulation

Centred stencils, either a fixed second-order Laplacian
(`wave2d_fd_manual`) or even orders 2–20 (`wave2d_fd`). The Laplacian
components are accumulated as *unscaled* stencil sums and multiplied by
$1/\Delta x^2$, $1/\Delta y^2$ in the model's right-hand side, which keeps the
stencil evaluator independent of the grid metric.

Time stepping is explicit, with the hyperbolic CFL condition

$$
\Delta t \;\lesssim\; \frac{1}{c}\left(\frac{1}{\Delta x^2}
                                     + \frac{1}{\Delta y^2}\right)^{-1/2}.
$$ {#eq-w2-cfl}

Note this is $\Delta t \sim \Delta x$, not the $\Delta x^2$ of a parabolic
problem: a wave equation is far less stiff than a diffusion equation at the
same resolution, and much less stiff than the high-order operators in the
spectral chapters.

## Verification

* **Runge–Kutta convergence.** Observed temporal order matches the scheme:
  halving $\Delta t$ reduces the error by roughly 4 for RK2 and by at least 8
  for RK4. The reference is *manufactured* — a fine-timestep RK4 run of the
  same code, not a closed-form solution — and the shipped drivers step with
  explicit Euler rather than either of these, so this measures the steppers,
  not the binaries.
* **Boundary mirrors.** The Dirichlet and Neumann ghost values are checked
  against hand-computed numbers, and an insufficient local extent is asserted
  to throw rather than silently produce wrong ghosts.
* **Golden checksum.** One pinned CPU literal (`wave2d-cpu-golden`), tied to a
  named machine and toolchain in its own comment.
* **Cross-implementation parity.** The padded manual path and the separated
  second-order path agree to $10^{-9}$.
* **Operator evaluation.** The Laplacian evaluator is checked against known
  inputs.
* **RHS structure.** Structural tests on the right-hand side pattern — API
  contracts rather than physics.
* **CPU–GPU parity.** Where GPU twins are built.

There is no analytical check anywhere in this application. Nothing compares the
computed field to a closed-form solution of @eq-w2-pde, and the CFL bound
@eq-w2-cfl is a textbook statement, not something the suite measures.

## Binaries and inputs

`wave2d_fd_manual`, `wave2d_fd`, plus `wave2d_cuda` / `wave2d_hip` when
enabled. Command-line driven, with optional VTK output (`--vtk`,
`--vtk-every`).

## Visualisation

![One Gaussian pulse, released at the centre of a $192\times96$ slab that is
periodic in $x$ and walled in $y$, run twice with **nothing changed but
`y_bc`**, and sampled at the same $t = 50$. The outgoing ring is identical in
both panels — same initial condition, same stepper, same 1000 steps — so
every difference is the wall. Look along the top and bottom edges. On the
left the Dirichlet (pressure-release) wall pins $u$ to zero and returns the
crest as a **trough**: the two darkest blue lobes, at $y \approx 15$ and
$y \approx 85$, are the reflected wave, inverted. On the right the Neumann
(rigid) wall returns it as a **crest**, and because the reflected and
incident waves add there, the deepest red in the figure sits against the
wall at nearly twice the incident amplitude. The colour scale is diverging
and centred on $u = 0$, and is shared between the panels, which is what
makes "inverted" legible as a colour flip rather than as two separately
normalised pictures. $t = 50$ rather than the end of the run: by $t = 70$
the two reflections have crossed in the middle and the slab is a reverberant
box, which is a different
question.](figures/wave2d_wall_reflection.svg){#fig-wave2d-walls}

## Scalability

Not measured.
